tldr: We present DreamMimic, a framework that enables humanoid robots to carry out vision-based whole-body loco-manipulation with high accuracy via world-model-assisted distillation. When transferring knowledge from a privileged teacher to a vision-based student policy, leveraging the world model's predictive latent dynamics significantly suppresses error accumulation in long-horizon, contact-rich tasks.
hero_caption: The overall framework of DreamMimic. Multiple expert teachers trained with privileged simulator information (such as exact object poses and contacts) are consolidated and distilled into a vision-based student policy via the world model's latent dynamics. In addition, Performance-Conditioned Guidance (PCG) adaptively balances teacher guidance based on the student's proficiency.
overview:
For humanoid robots to perform tasks in everyday spaces and factories, vision-based whole-body loco-manipulation—coordinating locomotion and object manipulation simultaneously using camera inputs—is essential. However, pushing or lifting objects involves discontinuous physical phenomena with frequent contact transitions. Moreover, camera images suffer from partial observability, where the back of the object or the moment of contact is occluded. While privileged simulator information (such as true 3D object poses and contact forces) allows us to train high-performing teacher policies, distilling (via imitation learning) this knowledge into a vision-based student policy deployable on real robots causes small prediction errors to snowball over time, leading to falls or dropped objects.

To address this, the authors developed DreamMimic, repurposing the Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM)—conventionally used for planning or imagination-based reinforcement learning—as a predictive feature extractor and a ruler for multi-step latent dynamics alignment in policy distillation. The world model predicts future latent states from the student's visual and proprioceptive history. In this latent space, multi-step constraints ensure that the future trajectory produced by the student's actions aligns with that of the teacher's actions. DreamMimic also introduces auxiliary prediction heads for contact states, object poses, and rewards, alongside a Performance-Conditioned Guidance (PCG) mechanism that automatically adjusts teacher intervention based on the student's mastery.

The framework was evaluated on large-scale human-object interaction datasets (OMOMO and BEHAVE) across long-horizon tasks such as carrying heavy tables, lifting chairs, and moving boxes. DreamMimic dramatically outperformed standard vision encoder baselines and single-stage world-model RL from pixels, achieving an impressive 92.2% success rate on OMOMO. Furthermore, its applicability to a different humanoid morphology (Unitree G1) and a different simulator (Isaac Sim) demonstrates that world models are a powerful tool for stabilizing visual humanoid control.
contributions: Repurposing the RSSM world model from planning to policy distillation, serving as a predictive feature space and an action-conditioned multi-step supervision signal for visual policies.

Introducing auxiliary prediction heads for contact labels, object states, privileged states, and rewards into the world model, encouraging the latent representation to retain signals essential for contact-rich interactions from visual history.

Proposing Performance-Conditioned Guidance (PCG), an adaptive distillation schedule that dynamically balances guidance and exploration based on the relative reward scores of the teacher and student, preventing premature teacher annealing and excessive interference.

Achieving tracking-based loco-manipulation performance that significantly surpasses strong vision baselines on OMOMO and BEHAVE datasets, while demonstrating robust transfer to the Unitree G1 robot and across different simulator environments.

sections.heading: Why is vision-based humanoid loco-manipulation so difficult, and how can world models help?
sections.summary: Whole-body loco-manipulation on humanoid robots is extremely hard to learn due to discontinuous contacts, high-dimensional action spaces, and partial observability from vision. While distillation from a privileged teacher is promising, error accumulation in long-horizon tasks often leads to failure. DreamMimic tackles this long-term drift problem at its root by leveraging a world model for predictive representation learning and multi-step alignment.
sections.details:
For humanoid robots to assist in factory automation and daily life, they must coordinate whole-body locomotion and manipulation using visual feedback. However, accurately capturing contact timing and bonding states from camera views alone is notoriously difficult, as the hands and body frequently occlude the line of sight.

Much prior research has focused on locomotion alone without object manipulation, or has relied on privileged information available only in simulation (such as ground-truth object poses and contact graphs). While distillation methods have been explored to compress these privileged policies into deployable vision-based controllers, standard single-step imitation learning suffers from compounding perception errors over time, eventually causing the robot to lose balance and fall.

Recently, world models (which predict environment dynamics in a latent space) have attracted attention in legged locomotion and autonomous driving, but their application to high-DOF, contact-rich whole-body humanoid manipulation has been scarce. Therefore, this work introduces DreamMimic, repurposing the RSSM (used in Dreamer) not for planning, but as a predictive representation backbone for the student policy and as a supervision signal to align multi-step action consequences with the teacher.

sections.heading: Prior work: physics-based character control, visual RL, and world models
sections.summary: This study sits at the intersection of physics-based whole-body character control, visual policy learning (teacher-student distillation), and world models for robotics. DreamMimic overcomes previous hurdles—reliance on privileged observations, instability in visual RL, and limitations of world models in high-contact tasks—using a novel distillation framework.
sections.details:
To place this paper in context, let us review three key areas:

- **Physics-based character control**: Reinforcement learning and imitation learning have recently enabled agile athletic movements in humanoid models. However, the bottleneck for real-world deployment has been the reliance on privileged observations. While prior work like InterMimic enabled large-scale training of privileged generalist policies, this study takes the next step: distilling them into a vision student operating strictly on onboard sensors.

- **Visual policy learning for robots**: Direct reinforcement learning from raw images is notoriously unstable due to high input dimensionality and delayed rewards. Imitation learning algorithms like DAgger and teacher-student distillation are effective, but distribution shift and compounding errors remain problematic under partial observability. This paper resolves this by pairing temporally consistent supervision from a world model with an adaptive guidance schedule (PCG) tied to student performance.

- **World models in robot control**: Frameworks like Dreamer and DayDreamer learn by imagining futures in latent space. However, on high-dimensional, contact-rich tasks like HumanoidBench, standalone learning from scratch often struggles. DreamMimic's unique angle is using the world model as a stabilizing guide for visual policy distillation rather than for direct policy optimization.

sections.heading: The core of DreamMimic: using world models as a distillation compass
sections.summary: The knowledge of a privileged teacher policy is distilled into a student policy driven only by onboard depth/segmentation images and proprioception. On the student side, an RSSM world model predicts future latent states, contacts, object poses, and rewards. These predictive features feed into the policy, while a constraint forces the future $H$-step latent trajectory to match the outcome of the teacher's actions.
sections.details:
DreamMimic's concrete architecture and training pipeline consist of the following components:

- **Problem formulation (POMDP)**: Without access to the simulator's true state $\boldsymbol{x}_t$, the robot receives only proprioceptive states $\boldsymbol{p}_t$ (such as joint states), depth and segmentation images, and a compact goal specification $\boldsymbol{g}_t$ (target object pose and end-effector keypoint targets).

- **Privileged teacher policy**: A set of expert policies trained via RL (PPO) in a privileged environment with full access to true object poses, contact graphs, and contact labels. Following InterMimic, diverse expert teachers cover various interaction scenarios.

- **Student policy input design**: The student policy network does not process raw images directly. Instead, the RSSM deterministic hidden state $\boldsymbol{h}_t$ encoded from visual and proprioceptive histories, along with predictions from auxiliary heads (predicted reward $\hat{r}_t$, privileged state $\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}^{\text{priv}}_t$, contact $\hat{\boldsymbol{c}}_t$, and object state $\hat{\boldsymbol{o}}^s_t$), are integrated via a lightweight Transformer and fed into the actor.

- **World model predictive learning and auxiliary heads**: The world model uses a Dreamer-style RSSM. In addition to reconstructing images and proprioceptive states (RecH), it features auxiliary prediction heads for task-critical variables like contacts and object poses. This ensures that the latent space strongly retains features required for contact-rich interaction.

- **Multi-step latent distillation**: Standard distillation only matches the current action $\boldsymbol{a}_t$. DreamMimic freezes the world model dynamics and penalizes the divergence ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{latent}}$) between the future $H$-step latent states $\boldsymbol{z}_{t+k}$ generated by the student's actions versus the teacher's actions (with $H=3$). This aligns the long-term consequences of actions with those of the teacher.

- **Performance-Conditioned Guidance (PCG)**: Rather than decaying the ratio $\rho$ of teacher-guided environments via a fixed schedule, PCG adaptively modulates it based on the ratio of moving-average rewards between student and teacher (relative performance). It offers strong guidance when the student is struggling, and encourages self-exploration as the student becomes proficient, ensuring stable training.

captions.F3: The overall architecture of the world model. It updates the deterministic state $h_t$ and stochastic state $s_t$ from observations. Beyond observation reconstruction, auxiliary prediction heads for contact (CPH), privileged state (RPH), object state (OSPH), and reward enrich the latent representation. The policy takes these predictive features to decide actions.

sections.heading: Experimental results: superior tracking stability and key ablation findings
sections.summary: Evaluated on two large-scale datasets, OMOMO and BEHAVE, DreamMimic achieved a 92.2% success rate on OMOMO, far surpassing baselines. Ablations confirmed the critical roles of multi-step latent supervision and auxiliary prediction heads. Stable behavior was also demonstrated on the Unitree G1 robot and across simulators in Isaac Sim.
sections.details:
Key experimental setups and findings are detailed below:

- **Evaluation setup and datasets**: Evaluated on the SMPL-X model (153 DOFs) using OMOMO (five object types including large tables, chairs, and plastic boxes) and BEHAVE (long sequences involving backpacks, containers, stools, etc.). Metrics include Success Rate (Succ.), Survival Time (Time), Robot Joint Error ($E_r$), and Object Tracking Error ($E_o$).

- **Quantitative evaluation (Tables I & II)**: On OMOMO, while direct encoder students (ResNet-18, ViT) and RL-only baselines struggled, DreamMimic achieved a 92.2% success rate. It maintained high tracking accuracy even under heavy-load stress tests with increased object masses. A single-stage Dreamer baseline trained directly from images slightly extended survival time, but rarely completed the high-contact, high-DOF tasks.

- **Ablation study (what drove performance?)**:
  - *Multi-step latent supervision*: Removing the $H=3$ step latent alignment caused the OMOMO success rate to drop sharply from 92.2% to 70.6%. This proves that single-step action matching is insufficient to curb long-term error drift.
  - *Auxiliary prediction heads*: Keeping only reconstruction loss (RecH) reduced the success rate to 86.3% and widened object tracking errors. Adding object state prediction significantly improved object tracking error from 12.7 cm to 8.8 cm.
  - *Predictive feature input to policy*: Using prediction heads only as auxiliary losses without feeding their features into the policy reduced the success rate to 84.3% (and down to 33.3% under heavy load).
  - *Distillation schedule (PCG)*: On BEHAVE, PCG clearly outperformed a naive epoch-based fixed decay schedule in both tracking error and survival duration.

- **Qualitative evaluation and generalization (Figs. 4, 5, 6)**: While baselines lost balance and fell when lifting objects, DreamMimic stably lifted tables and continued walking. Furthermore, stable whole-body interaction was verified on the 42-DOF Unitree G1 humanoid (Fig. 5) and in cross-simulator zero-shot transfer from Isaac Gym to Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab (Fig. 6).

- **Failure mode analysis**: Failures still occurred under extreme occlusions that created camera blind spots, or when contact points were visually ambiguous. On the Unitree G1, insufficient upper-body grip strength occasionally caused the robot to regress from lifting to pushing heavy objects.

captions.F4: Qualitative comparison on contact-rich loco-manipulation. Top: DreamMimic; bottom: ResNet-18 baseline. DreamMimic maintains balance while lifting and carrying a large table, whereas the baseline fails to establish stable contact and falls.
captions.F5: Qualitative comparison on the Unitree G1 robot (42 DOFs) in Isaac Gym. DreamMimic (top) stably pushes a box while maintaining balance, whereas the single-stage Dreamer baseline (bottom) destabilizes and falls upon contact.
captions.F6: Zero-shot cross-simulator transfer in Isaac Sim. The DreamMimic policy trained in Isaac Gym executes complex whole-body interactions with wooden chairs and large tables stably in Isaac Sim.

sections.heading: Takeaway: world models act as a stabilizer for visual whole-body control
sections.summary: This study introduced DreamMimic, which leverages the latent dynamics of world models to stably distill vision-based humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation. Combining multi-step latent alignment to counter long-term drift, auxiliary heads to capture interaction dynamics, and an adaptive guidance schedule (PCG) yields high tracking performance on challenging tasks.
sections.details:
By shifting the role of world models from planning tools to stabilizers for representation learning and multi-step distillation, DreamMimic brings a fresh breakthrough to visual control for contact-rich, high-DOF humanoid robots.

This framework transfers the high motor capabilities of privileged simulation teachers to partially observable camera students without degradation, marking an important step toward real-world humanoid deployment. Future directions include improving robustness against occlusions in real-world cameras, integrating tactile sensing, and coordinating with fine-grained dexterous force control.

takeaways: RSSM world models function effectively not just for planning, but as multi-step latent alignment signals and predictive feature extractors in imitation learning.
In vision-based, long-horizon contact tasks, single-step action matching is inadequate; penalizing the divergence of future latent states caused by actions is critical.

Dynamically adjusting teacher-student guidance based on real-time relative reward scores (PCG) provides greater stability without relying on sensitive hyperparameter tuning compared to fixed-step decay.
Auxiliary tasks predicting privileged states and contact labels encourage the world model's latent space to preserve geometric and physical features vital for contact-rich manipulation.
limitations: All experiments were conducted in simulation environments (Isaac Gym / Isaac Sim) and lack physical validation on real humanoid hardware.
The method assumes clean depth and segmentation images as inputs; its robustness against real-world camera noise and imperfect perception pipelines remains unverified.
Under extreme occlusions where the hands are completely hidden behind an object, world model prediction accuracy drops, occasionally leading to task failure.
Due to motion retargeting limitations, actual robot models like the Unitree G1 may lack sufficient grip force, leading lifting motions to regress into pushing.
